Most of the FOMC-induced yield changes accelerated after the Fed's large-scale asset purchases at the start of the Financial Crisis in 2008, suggesting that the Fed may have been leaning against the fiscal wind. See Hall and Sargent (2022) who compare U.S. fiscal and monetary policy during the pandemic and the world wars. While the systematic price responses around the cost releases suggest that they contain fiscal news relevant to Treasury investors, we would also like to distinguish the impact of the bill's cash flow news from potential revisions in the bill's enactment probability. To better isolate cash flow news, we focus on the subset of spending proposals with the emergency designation. Emergency spending bills are unfunded and typically have strong bipartisan support. Congress has increasingly used the emergency designation to circumvent budget rules over the past few decades, even outside crises. 3 Strong bipartisan support implies that the ex-ante probability that these emergency proposals are enacted is close to one, allowing us to better isolate the expected cash flows for the proposal. Bypassing budget rules implies that there are no expected fiscal offsets over the budgeting horizon (i.e., 5-10 years) to fund these emergency bills, implying that the cost estimates are more likely to capture the direct cash flow impact of the bill in the near term.

We extract deficit news by taking revisions from consecutive cost estimates within an emergency proposal. Before any formal CBO cost release, investors may form expectations about these cost estimates. For larger emergency bills, we often observe an approximate dollar figure publicly circulated before the first formal CBO cost release, allowing investors to anchor their expectations about the size of the bill. We obtain these informal estimates from White House requests, Congressional committees, leadership negotiations, or media reports preceding the first public CBO report. We then compute the cash flow revision in the first CBO cost release relative to these informal estimates to obtain a full set of revisions that we interpret as cash flow surprises within a bill. Regressing Treasury values and yields on our cash flow surprise measure, we find that a one-time 1% increase in the present value of deficits scaled by GDP over the budgeting horizon corresponds to a 0.75 bps increase in 10-year nominal yields after one day. This point estimate is conservative because the effect grows to approximately 2 bps after one week as the event window expands. Given a deficit persistence of 0.9, this implies a cumulative increase in yields of approximately 6.75 bps (≈ 0.75 × 0.9/(1 -0.9)) to 18 bps (≈ 2 × 0.9/(1 -0.9)) in response to a 1% increase in the deficit-to-GDP ratio.

To further contextualize these estimates, we compute the revisions in the present value of deficits from the CBO Long-term Budget Outlook reports. The 2023 report (projecting deficits from 2023 to 2053) indicates a 246% increase, while the 1997 report (projecting deficits from 1997 to 2031) implies a -7.01% change, resulting in a total increase of 253% of GDP. Applying our elasticity estimates, this change corresponds to an increase in 10-year nominal yields of at least 1.95 percentage points. It is important to note that the Treasury response reflects any cash flow news from the individual bill and any aggregate news about surpluses or government discount rates conveyed in the cost releases. The first part of our analysis has focused on extracting cash flow news only about the individual proposal from the cost releases. However, the cash flow revision may not only be attributed to an additive shock but could be due to revisions in the policy rule. The second part entertains this possibility by allowing for the cost releases to reveal changes to the aggregate fiscal stance or long-run expectations of fiscal offsets (which relate to aggregate surpluses or discount rates). Our CBO sample occurs in an unusual period of the U.S. fiscal history, marked by a radical departure in its fiscal stance. We show that professional analysts had not predicted the drift in deficits at the start of our sample but had to learn about it using incoming data.

We find persistent biases and continual downward revisions in analyst forecasts inconsistent with a standard full information rational expectations (FIRE) framework. Analysts strongly revise their forecasts about surpluses downwards around the large negative cost releases, aligning with the yield increases on these days. In addition to providing cash flow news about individual proposals, the analyst forecasts, therefore, suggest that the cost releases are also informative signals about the trend in aggregate deficits. We relax full information and allow the cost releases to contain news about the pure additive cash flow component and revisions in the policy parameters and states from Bayesian learning in a present value framework. We capture the fiscal stance at two different horizons. The policy parameters governing surpluses and government discount rates over the 10-year budgeting horizon capture the near-term fiscal stance, while the parameters governing the expected debt burden in 10 years capture the long-run fiscal stance (e.g., long-term expectations of tax increases or spending cuts arising from a fiscal consolidation). Given the sharp departure from the fiscal discipline in the 1990s, investors initially assigned a low probability to the actual path of rising deficits over the subsequent decades. A high intensity of large negative cost releases corresponded to a sequence of deficit shocks and allowed investors to learn about the loosening of fiscal policy, reinforcing the devaluation of Treasurys. We also find that investors expected that some of the near-term deficit news over the budgeting horizon would eventually be offset by long-run tax increases or spending cuts (57 cents of every dollar in the fiscal expansion is passed through to Treasury valuations). Running regressions with model-implied data suggests that a 1% increase in the present value of deficits scaled by GDP over the 10-year budgeting horizon corresponds to a 3.39 bps decline in Treasury values, and assuming a Treasury portfolio duration of four years, this implies a 0.85 bps rise in nominal yields, both consistent with our empirical estimates. Our model attributes a significant portion of the deficit news from cost releases to revisions in policy parameters that reinforce the negative cash flow shocks.

We relate to the empirical literature linking government debt valuations to surplus news using budget identities (e.g., Berndt, Lustig, and Yeltekin (2012), Jiang, Lustig, Van Nieuwerburgh, and Xiaolan (2024a), Cochrane (2022), Coibion, Gorodnichenko, and Weber (2021), and Hilscher, Raviv, and Reis (2022)). We distinguish our paper by exploiting high-frequency and granular data about the cash flows of individual legislative proposals to isolate when bond investors learn about future surpluses, evidenced by the significant response of Treasury valuations to cost releases in daily event windows. Jiang, Lustig, Van Nieuwerburgh, and Xiaolan (2024b) do not find evidence that Treasury values respond to news about future surpluses using aggregate data at a quarterly frequency. We provide suggestive evidence that the actions of the Fed may have been counteracting the effects of these fiscal shocks over our sample, making it challenging to identify the effect of surplus news on Treasury values at lower frequencies. Our paper contributes to the small but growing literature on the pricing of fiscal risk in bond markets (Dai and Philippon, 2005;Bretscher, Hsu, and Tamoni, 2020;Corhay, Kind, Kung, and Morales, 2023). We find that large negative proposals steepen the term structure, consistent with Bretscher et al. (2020)'s findings that government spending predicts bond excess returns. While there is a large literature on high-frequency identification of the effects of monetary policy shocks on interest rates and bond yields, especially around FOMC announcements starting with Kuttner (2001); Cochrane and Piazzesi (2002); Nakamura and Steinsson (2018), our paper is the first to use this approach for fiscal shocks. 4Our approach to measuring surplus news at the bill level and extracting relevant information from cost projections builds on the narrative approach to constructing fiscal shocks (e.g., Romer and Romer (2010), Ramey (2011), Mertens and Ravn (2012), Guajardo, Leigh, and Pescatori (2014), Alesina, Favero, and Giavazzi (2019), Drautzburg (2020), Bianchi, Gómez-Cram, and Kung (2024), and Hazell and Hobler (2024)). We show that the CBO cost projections at the bill level reveal fiscal news with significant pricing implications.

In our model, bond investors learn about long-run dynamics in macroeconomic data (e.g., see Croce, Lettau, and Ludvigson, 2015;Collin-Dufresne, Johannes, and Lochstoer, 2016;Gomez Cram and Lawrence, 2024;Kozlowski, Veldkamp, and Venkateswaran, 2020;Johannes, Lochstoer, and Mou, 2016;Farmer, Nakamura, and Steinsson, 2024;Giacoletti, Laursen, and Singleton, 2021;Li, Van Nieuwerburgh, and Renxuan, 2025). We build on this literature by showing that Bayesian investors who are learning about the persistent trend in deficits through incoming cost releases in a present value framework can generate bond price drifts. In traditional macro models, monetary policy has a small influence on long-term real rates. To anchor short rates, central bankers rely on measures of the equilibrium real rate that are assumed to be invariant with respect to monetary policy (See, e.g., work by Laubach and Williams, 2003;Holston, Laubach, and Williams, 2017, on rstar). Recently, there has been more evidence that monetary policy impacts long-term real rates (Hanson and Stein, 2015;Hillenbrand, 2025;Bianchi, Lettau, and Ludvigson, 2022). Our findings suggest that the Fed may have been actively neutralizing the effect of fiscal news on long-term real rates, especially after the Financial Crisis in 2008.

This section first describes the information provided by the cost estimates of individual legislative proposals from Congress. We then provide a present value framework for interpreting the news content in the cost estimates.

The Congressional Budget Act of 1974 (CBA) established centralized budgeting with revenue and spending targets specified in the budget resolution. The CBA also created the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), which is a non-partisan agency that provides hundreds of cost estimates of legislative proposals and other budgetary information each year. The CBO is legally required to provide cost estimates for a legislative proposal after committee approval but before it is voted on by the full Senate and House. 5 These cost estimates are designed to calculate the impact of legislative proposals on the federal budget across multiple years. The CBO promotes transparency by posting cost estimates on its website (cbo.gov), granting access to members of Congress, their staff, and the public. Congress can use these estimates to enforce budget rules. The CBO gets a unique glimpse of the legislative path of a given proposal before the public cost release. 6 For example, CBO analysts have direct access to the legislators of the bill to gather specific details of the scale and implementation of the bill used to prepare the estimates. The analysts also provide confidential cost estimates of alternative legislative options in the early stages of the bill and before the public cost release to help guide the congressional committee in selecting the legislative path for the bill. In that sense, the public cost estimates reflect private information about legislators' preferences regarding the size and scope of the bill.

We analyze all legislative proposals introduced by Congress covering the 105th Congress (1997Congress ( -1998) ) to the 117th Congress (2021-2022), yielding 15,050 unique proposals. Our sample starts in 1997 because that is when the cost releases began to comprehensively cover all proposed legislation. For each bill, we obtained the CBO published cost estimate along with any updates in the cost estimates, detailing the projected cash flow effects of the proposed legislation on three key components of the federal budget for the current year and the subsequent five to ten years: discretionary spending, mandatory (or direct) spending, and federal revenues. 7 These cost estimates provide a comprehensive coverage of legislative proposals, including policy agendas, major budgetary events (e.g., Reconciliations, Consolidated Appropriations, Supplemental Appropriations), and revisions in budget rules. From each cost estimate document, we collect the net surplus impact by year, bill number, title, legislative status, and publication date. We augment the data gathered from the cost estimate document with key legislative actions and corresponding dates (i.e., when the bill was first introduced in the House and Senate, committee meetings, congressional vote, and if the bill was signed into law by the president) from congress.gov. p.s: Measuring the effects of large deficit proposals
p.t: The regression evidence suggests that cost estimates contain fiscal news. This subsection shows that the news in our cost estimates is concentrated among proposals projected to considerably increase deficits if enacted. Treasury values decline significantly following these cost releases, attributed to higher expected inflation and nominal term premia and lower convenience yields, as reported in Subsection 2.1.3. We classify legislative proposals into binary categories by sign (positive and negative) and by size (small and large) based on the cash flow contribution measure. We first categorize proposals into those with positive and negative values of cbo (z) t+∆t separately. Within each sign category, we rank proposals with the largest cash flow contribution in absolute value (i.e., |cbo (z) t+∆t |) in a 3-month rolling window. We then define large proposals as those exceeding the median absolute value in each sign category, yielding large positive and large negative subsets of proposals. Using a rolling window avoids lookahead bias in our selection criteria. 10 Our identification assumption is that the change in Treasury values on days when there is a large proposal is dominated by the news content of the cost release, as small bills likely have a negligible impact on Treasuries given their minimal effect on the budget. In all of our tests, we exclude all large proposal days that coincide with a three-day window around FOMC meeting days. The rationale for excluding these days is that FOMC meeting days might drive the variation of bond returns on those days. We also show that our results are robust to excluding days with large macro announcements. 11

This section focuses on a subset of the proposals that allow us to extract a direct measure of the cash flow surprises. We focus on spending proposals with an emergency designation. These bills are exempt from budget rules (i.e., unfunded), typically have strong bipartisan support, and are fast-tracked. The strong bipartisan support and quick passage suggest a high ex-ante probability that the emergency bills will be passed, allowing us to better isolate the deficit news in the cost releases from potential revisions in the enactment probability. Bypassing budget rules eliminates expectations of near-term fiscal offsets, making their cost estimates more likely to reflect the full budgetary impact. There has been a significant increase in the share of emergency spending in both the discretionary and mandatory categories in our sample period, allowing Congress to circumvent budget rules and contribute to the rising deficits. For example, emergency spending accounted for around 10% of discretionary spending in the past decade. The rise in emergency spending is a reflection of the gradual erosion of fiscal discipline over the past few decades. We have 39 unique emergency spending bills in our sample, with an average of two CBO cost estimates for each bill, allowing us to compute revisions within a proposal as it evolves through the lawmaking process. These bills have strong bipartisan support, averaging 283 and 66 yea votes in the House and Senate, respectively, representing 68% support in each chamber. Bills require a simple majority to pass (218 votes in the House, 51 in the Senate), though Senate filibusters often necessitate 60 votes and expedited procedures can require a two-thirds majority. They also move quickly through Congress, averaging 168 days (149 median) from introduction to passage, compared to 275 days (247 median) for other bills.

3 News about the fiscal stance The previous section focused on extracting cash flow news about the individual proposal from the cost releases. We now entertain the possibility that the cash flow shock is partly driven by revisions in the aggregate fiscal stance. In the context of the present value decomposition from equation (4), we now consider that the cost estimates provide informative signals about underlying trends in aggregate deficits and government discount rates (in addition to the cash flows about the individual proposal). Our CBO sample occurs in an unusual period of the U.S. fiscal history, marked by a radical departure in its fiscal stance. Figure 8 plots the federal surplus to GDP ratio with our sample period highlighted in gray, illustrating the extraordinary drift in deficits and a significant reversal of the fiscal consolidations in the 1990s. We argue that it was unlikely for investors to have anticipated this persistent trend. We first show that professional analysts had not predicted the drift in deficits at the start of our sample but had to learn about it using incoming data. We find persistent biases and continual downward revisions in analyst forecasts inconsistent with a standard full information rational expectations (FIRE) framework. Table B.13 in the Appendix demonstrates that Economic Consensus forecasts about the budget exhibit several common forecast anomalies suggesting deviations from FIRE beyond bias and constant downward revisions. The forecast errors are autocorrelated, they deviate from one-for-one movements with actual realizations as demonstrated by Mincer-Zarnowitz regressions (Mincer and Zarnowitz, 1969), and they display underreaction to new information as revealed by Coibion-Gorodnichenko regressions (Coibion and Gorodnichenko, 2015). In standard FIRE models, investors know the model describing the budgetary process (e.g., cash flow and discount rate dynamics) and observe all corresponding parameters, states, and shocks. Based on observable information, agents form expectations as statistically optimal forecasts that are correct on average and equal to realizations. In this sample, it seems implausible to assume that investors knew the full model governing the dynamics of the surplus. Investors in 1997 were unlikely to anticipate the unprecedented drift in deficits over the next 25 years, but instead had to learn about the persistent loosening of fiscal policy using incoming data. We entertain departures from full information next in an estimated present value framework where Bayesian investors need to recursively learn about the fiscal stance. This framework allows the cost releases to contain news about the pure additive cash flow component and revisions in the policy parameters and states. Anchoring prior beliefs at the start of our sample using past data, investors initially assigned a low probability to the path of increasing deficits materializing in our sample, which marked a significant departure from past policy. A high intensity of large negative cost releases corresponded to a sequence of deficit shocks and allow investors to learn about the loosening of fiscal policy, reinforcing the devaluation of Treasurys.

We model the fiscal stance at two different horizons. The unobservable persistent components of surplus policy and government discount rates over the 10-year budgeting horizon capture the near-term fiscal stance, while the unobservable components of the expected debt burden 10-years from now capture the long-run fiscal stance (e.g., long-run expectations of tax increases or spending cuts). Bond investors learn about the stance of future policy at these two different horizons using incoming data from CBO cost releases, realized surpluses, and bond price data. We find that the cost releases enable investors to learn about the parameters governing the fiscal policy. Parameter learning is slow, given the significant persistence and magni-tude of the departure in fiscal policy, which is akin to rational agents gradually learning about the unobservable persistent components of the nominal short rate highlighted in Farmer et al. (2024). Investors at the start of our CBO data sample in 1997 would have observed a significant budget consolidation throughout the 1990s and found the reversal and subsequent drift in policy over the next few decades to be unlikely. We show that a high intensity of large negative cost releases corresponds to a long sequence of negative cash flow shocks. Since these cash flow realizations are highly unlikely given the investors' prior, they lead investors to revise parameter estimates, amplifying the negative impact of deficit shocks on Treasury values in our model. The model can also reproduce insignificant Treasury value changes to large positive proposals.

The model estimation implies that the negative Treasury value responses to large negative cost releases reflect investors updating their beliefs about the aggregate surplus process that reinforces the effects of the cash flow shocks. When investors observe periods with a high concentration of proposals related to spending increases or tax cuts, we show that the cost releases provide valuable signals about a drift toward a more profligate stance in fiscal policy.

We document that revisions in CBO cost projections about legislative proposals contain valuable news about the deficit impact of the individual bill and the aggregate fiscal stance. We find the largest negative Treasury value responses on days with large cost releases associated with major net spending bills. The Treasury response is related to an increase in expected inflation and nominal term premia, along with a decrease in convenience yields. We exploit a subset of the cost releases pertaining to emergency proposals to extract deficit news. Emergency proposals are unfunded and have a high ex-ante probability of passing, allowing us to better isolate the cash flow news component. The Treasury value responses are magnified by a factor of three for cost revisions relating to emergency spending proposals. We then allow for the possibility that the cost releases contain news about the additive cash flow shock as well as information about the aggregate fiscal stance, including long-run fiscal offsets. To this end, we develop a present-value model in which Bayesian investors use the incoming cost releases as signals about the size of Congress' legislative wish list to learn about the policy parameters and states governing surpluses, discount rates, and expected future Treasury supply. An increasing frequency and size of spending proposals in our sample corresponded to a sequence of deficit shocks and caused investors to revise their beliefs about the loosening of fiscal policy, reinforcing the decline in Treasury values.

We use real-time data from the Bloomberg Professional Service to account for macroeconomic news. Specifically, we control for macroeconomic news releases by computing the difference between the realized value and the expected value of macroeconomic indicator k at time t, denoted A kt and E kt respectively. We standardize this difference by dividing it by the sample standard deviation of A kt -E kt , denoted σk , following the approach in Balduzzi, Elton, and Green (2001), and Bianchi, Gómez-Cram, Kind, and Kung (2023): This standardization allows us to compare indicators with different units of measurement but it does not affect the statistical significance of our estimates, as σk is constant for any given indicator. To obtain the expected value E kt for each indicator, we use the median forecast from the most recent weekly survey of economists conducted by Bloomberg prior to the announcement. p.t: This section relates the bill-level cost estimates with the CBO's aggregate surplus projections. One of CBO's mandated obligations is to produce the annual Budget and Economic Outlook, presenting baseline projections of the surplus or deficit for the upcoming decade. This report is typically published at the beginning of the year and undergoes revisions in March and July. The baseline projections are not intended as forecasts of budgetary or economic outcomes; rather, they represent the CBO's assessment of how the budget and the economy would evolve under existing laws. Hence, the baseline serves as a reference point for evaluating the potential effects of proposed legislation. The remaining 44% of the variance in surplus changes is equally accounted for by the second and third categories, namely economic changes and technical changes. Economic changes arise from revisions made to the agency's economic forecast, which includes adjustments to incorporate the macroeconomic effects of recently enacted legislation.
